note: The primer most clinicians have actually read, which makes it the right shared reference in client conversations.
title: Large language models in medicine
explain_beginner: The question, stepping back from any one specific model, what is the realistic role for large language models in medicine as a whole, what can they genuinely help with right now, and what makes them risky to lean on. This review appeared at a moment when language models were suddenly capable of passing medical licensing style exam questions, which understandably generated a great deal of excitement, but passing a written exam is a different thing from being safe to use with real patients, and the authors wanted to draw that distinction clearly for a broad medical readership. The authors describe genuine near term value in tasks like turning free text radiology reports into structured, standardized reports, pulling relevant information out of a patient's clinical notes, and drafting discharge summaries, while also documenting specific hazards, models that state false information fluently and confidently, models that reproduce harmful stereotypes absorbed from training text, and a lack of transparency in how any given answer was reached. What it does not settle, performing well on exam style questions does not tell you how a model will behave with an ambiguous, messy real patient case, and the review does not resolve who is accountable when a language model contributes to a bad clinical outcome.
explain_business: This review supports prioritizing documentation and information extraction tasks, structuring radiology reports, drafting discharge summaries, pulling facts from clinical notes, as the safer near term entry point for adopting language models in a clinical setting, over direct diagnostic or treatment decision use. The point that these models cannot meet standard authorship or accountability criteria is directly relevant to liability planning, since if a language model contributes to an error, responsibility still has to rest with the supervising clinician or institution rather than the model itself, and organizations should make that chain of accountability explicit before any deployment. Strong performance on licensing exam questions should not be read by a buyer as evidence of general clinical readiness, since the review explicitly treats exam performance as a weaker signal than real world task performance under ambiguous conditions. Data privacy handling for any tool trained on or processing patient records needs separate legal review, since the paper flags this as a live, unresolved concern rather than something existing tools have already solved. This is relevant now for organizations piloting documentation support, treating the model as an aid a clinician reviews rather than a decision maker.
explain_practitioner: Method, a narrative review of large language model capabilities and limitations for clinical use, covering education, documentation, information extraction, and research support applications, built from the published literature available in 2023 rather than new original benchmarking. The review highlights strong performance on medical licensing style exam questions as an early proof point of capability, and specific practical applications including converting unstructured radiology report text into structured formats and extracting relevant information from electronic health records and clinical notes to support documentation tasks like discharge summaries. Exam question performance is treated explicitly as a weak proxy for real clinical readiness, since exam questions are a controlled, simplified task compared with the ambiguity of live patient care, a distinction the authors draw deliberately rather than treating exam scores as the headline result. The authors identify hallucination, the generation of fluent but factually false content, as a central risk, alongside bias where models have been shown to associate certain demographic groups with negative stereotypes including violence, a black box lack of explainability that makes it hard to trace how an answer was produced, data privacy concerns tied to processing sensitive health information, and an accountability gap since language models cannot fulfill standard authorship or responsibility criteria.
